newsitem.title: UK: Blair faces tough time selling IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Blair faces tough time selling IRA ceasefire.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair faces a tough battle to persuade Northern Ireland's Protestant Unionist politicians that the IRA is genuine in ordering a ceasefire.
"IRA calls a truce - now the hard work begins," said the headline in the Observer newspaper, echoing the caution that greeted the guerrilla group's announcement.
The jubilation and relief that heralded the last Irish Republican Army ceasefire in August 1994 were starkly absent this time.

"Obviously we will want to assess the ceasefire with great care," said Blair, stepping into a political minefield as he tried to solve one of the most intractable guerrilla conflicts of the 20th century.

The Unionists, who fervently insist that Britain must maintain its links with Northern Ireland, fear Blair may have sold out to the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, in his eagerness to kickstart stalled peace talks.
Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble, who sees Blair on Monday for a crucial meeting that could decide the fate of the talks, knows that he faces the biggest risk of his political career.

"If he stays in talks...he could be crucified by hardliners. But if he walks away, he will be vilified as a wrecker of the best opportunity for securing a lasting peace settlement in Northern Ireland in decades," The Observer said.
Blair does at least have one political trump card to play after his landslide election victory in May.
For he is under none of the pressures forced on his Conservative predecessor John Major who needed Unionist support to maintain his tenuous hold on power at the head of a minority government.
The British media did not interpret the IRA's decision to start a ceasefire from noon on Sunday as a final milestone on the road to peace after a 28-year conflict that has claimed 3,200 lives.
"By giving more ground, Mr Blair has gone the extra mile for peace...He has, in the process, taken a big risk," The Sunday Times said. "We must be thankful for renewed peace and hold our breath."

The Independent newspaper said the peace talks would now be imbued with steely realism but noted: "There was no dancing in the streets or singing in the saloons. On the contrary, the mood was sceptical, sombre even."
Perhaps the bluntest reaction came from a victim of the 1996 London bomb that ended the last IRA ceasefire, killed two people and caused 400 million pounds ($670 million) worth of damage.

Alistair Cook, still picking glass out of the carpet 17 months after the Docklands bomb shattered his tower block apartment, said: "They are a bunch of bastards and I don't believe anything they say."
